scenes.visual: Title card: Species on the Move. Silent, 3 seconds.

scenes.tts: As the climate warms, species are on the move. Across many studies of land species, ranges have shifted toward the poles and up mountains, by a median of about seventeen kilometres and eleven metres every decade. Species vary a lot around those numbers. In the sea, species have moved poleward about six times faster. That reshuffling is already changing which species live together, and it matters for ecosystems and for people.
scenes.visual: A globe with species dots drifting poleward, arrows of very different lengths; then a mountain with dots climbing; then sea dots moving faster.

scenes.tts: How do we know? In twenty eleven, I-Ching Chen, Chris Thomas and colleagues pooled published range shifts into one meta-analysis. Shifts were biggest where the climate had warmed the most. Poleward shifts roughly kept pace with warming. Uphill shifts mostly fell short. The lesson's worked problem shows how to measure that shortfall on a mountain.
scenes.visual: Many small study cards merge into one plot: bigger shifts where warming was bigger; a short uphill arrow beside a longer isotherm arrow.

scenes.tts: Why does it matter? Species do not move together, so communities come apart and reassemble. Hosts and pathogens can meet in new places. A twenty seventeen review traced the effects of these moves to food production, the spread of disease, and how much carbon land and sea store.
scenes.visual: A community of icons splits as some leave and others arrive; three chips appear: food, disease, carbon.
scenes.narration: Why does it matter? Species do not move together, so communities come apart and reassemble. Hosts and pathogens can meet in new places. A 2017 review traced the effects of these moves to food production, the spread of disease, and how much carbon land and sea store.

scenes.tts: Climate is not acting alone. Clearing land for farms and towns is the largest single driver of biodiversity loss on land. One model estimate put the average loss of local species richness at thirteen point six percent. In warmer regions, forest loss also tended to speed up uphill shifts. And species carried by people are among the most common threats linked to extinctions.
scenes.visual: Forest edge cleared into fields; a richness bar shrinks; a species dot on a cleared slope moves up; a ship and a plane carry species between continents.

scenes.tts: Warming also shifts timing. Many spring events now come earlier, but not by the same amount for every species. When a bird's breeding moves less than its caterpillar food, chicks can miss the peak. In Dutch pied flycatchers, populations fell by about ninety percent where caterpillars peaked early. Fewer chicks do not always mean fewer birds, though.
scenes.visual: Two timelines, bird laying and caterpillar peak, sliding apart; a population bar falls in an early-peak forest and holds in a late-peak forest.

scenes.tts: In the sea, dissolved carbon dioxide lowers pH and the carbonate that shells and skeletons are built from. On average, calcification, growth and survival fall, but groups differ widely. On land, nitrogen from polluted air can cut plant diversity. On Minnesota prairie, a modest extra dose lowered species number by seventeen percent.
scenes.visual: Carbon dioxide bubbles into seawater; carbonate ions decline beside a shell; then nitrogen falls on a prairie plot and a few tall plants crowd out the rest.

scenes.tts: So when a range moves uphill, that shows a change happened. Scientists call that detection. It does not show the cause. Attribution links the change to a cause, and tests the alternatives, such as forest loss. Test the alternatives before you name the cause.
